pr_title: Handle X509 policy constraints on macOS.
pr_body:
This handles the "PolicyConstraints" chain building status for macOS, which will currently cause an exception to be thrown. Like name constraints, macOS does not have a separate error for the violation type as Windows does.

There are two policy constraint related statuses, `NoIssuanceChainPolicy` and `InvalidPolicyConstraints`. macOS maps the error to the latter. Both of these are covered under `X509VerificationFlags.IgnoreInvalidPolicy` already.

As of right now, OpenSSL appears to be effectively ignoring policy constraint violations. Enabling policy constraint checks with OpenSSL appeared to have unintended consequences, so it is left disabled for now, as it currently is.

Closes #46585

issue_context.title: X.509 chain building throws on macOS with policy constraint violations
issue_context.body:
Another chain status we aren't handling for macOS is a "PolicyConstraints", or when a certificate chain violates the policy as defined in 2.5.29.36.

Found this one by looking for it, it is not new in Big Sur or started running in to it.

Need to research how Windows / Linux react to this situation.

OpenSSL won't do anything unless we specify `X509_V_FLAG_POLICY_CHECK`. Depending on what Windows does:

1. If Windows also enforces policy checks, then:
    1.  make macOS report it as Windows does
    2. Enable it for OpenSSL
2. If Windows does not enforce it, then:
    1. Ignore it for macOS
Meh. Windows breaks down policy violations to `NoIssuanceChainPolicy`, `InvalidPolicyConstraints`, etc depending on the scenario.

On Linux we should be getting it from https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates/src/Internal/Cryptography/Pal.Unix/CertificatePolicy.cs

Assuming, of course, that the class works correctly it seems like it'd be easy enough to add it to the Apple pipeline (if it isn't there already) and ignore the native code.

@bartonjs Hm, I was looking more at the internal chain building mechanisms, not the managed one. Windows and macOS both enforce policy constraints in the presence of a 2.5.29.36 extension when requireExplicitPolicy is violated.

> On Linux we should be getting it from

If Linux is meant to be checking policy enforcement today, that does not seem to be the case.

Adding `X509_V_FLAG_POLICY_CHECK` to here gets policy checking similarly to Windows / macOS:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/d448461805e68566a33611acccf7589dad73976a/src/libraries/Native/Unix/System.Security.Cryptography.Native/pal_x509.c#L233

> Adding X509_V_FLAG_POLICY_CHECK to here gets policy checking similarly to Windows / macOS:

Hm. I feel like there was a reason I couldn't or didn't use that in the past, but instead wrote the CertificatePolicy class.  Maybe it wasn't available on 0.9.8 (which was in support at the time)?  Or maybe it was like macOS and didn't give the codes separated the Windows way.

Or maybe I'm only thinking about what happens when there's a value specified in ChainPolicy.ApplicationPolicy or ChainPolicy.CertificatePolicy, and this is about chain consistency, and we just want to use the flag.

So nice that we have a framework for writing tests for these things now :smile:.

> Or maybe I'm only thinking about what happens when there's a value specified in ChainPolicy.ApplicationPolicy or ChainPolicy.CertificatePolicy, and this is about chain consistency, and we just want to use the flag.

This seems the most plausible.

> So nice that we have a framework for writing tests for these things now.

Indeed. The dynamic chain and revocation tests are extremely helpful.

> Adding X509_V_FLAG_POLICY_CHECK to here gets policy checking similarly to Windows / macOS

Hm. It appears I was mistaken exactly as to what this flag does. Policy checking in OpenSSL and Windows appears to be rather different from how it is done in Windows and MacOS.

review_comments: Perhaps a test where the sequence is empty?
(Maybe it's not needed, but it's sort of a "there's one test for garbage data, do we need to care if this edge case is garbage on all platforms?")

Mayyybe? The test for the malformed data is for the policy constraint extension, not the policy identifier extension. 

I'm also not entirely sure how much "documenting" of OS-specific behavior we want to do in tests. For example, right now macOS does not error if this sequence is empty, assuming there is no other reason for it to error. If a later macOS version changed it to start throwing because they started doing tighter asn.1 validation, would we be able to, or care enough, to make changes to the product code to fix the test? Or we just "fix" the test and say "we defer to the platform"?

If the latter, then it feels like writing tests more against the OS than .NET.
Yep, makes sense, and probably the position I'd've had if I wrote the code instead of read the code.
